imperial.name: Tomato, Greenhouse

actions.text:
Plant under glass

Apr–May once warm.

Sow indoors

Late Feb–Mar. Late Jan only with a heated greenhouse and bright light.

Containers

One per 12–18 in. pot, two per standard growbag.

Bed spacing

18–24 in., wider for vigorous cordons.

methods.text:
Sow indoors 

Sow thinly in trays or small pots of seed compost at about 64°F. Keep moist and give emerging seedlings plenty of light.

Prick out and pot on 

Move tray seedlings into pots at their first pair of true leaves. Support the roots and hold a leaf. Pot on as the roots fill the pot.

Plant in the greenhouse 

Wait until nights stay around 50°F or warmer. Water well-rooted plants and set them slightly deeper in pots, growbags or an enriched bed. Stand cordon pots 24 in. apart centre to centre. Support plants with canes or string.

varieties.text:
CHERRY AND SMALL FRUITED
Sungold F1

A vigorous cordon tomato with very sweet orange cherry fruits. A strong first choice for greenhouse snacking and salads.

ORDINARY
Alicante

A traditional red salad tomato grown as a cordon. Retain as an accessible, general-purpose greenhouse variety.

F1 HYBRID
Shirley

An early cordon tomato producing medium red fruits under glass. A familiar, practical choice for an unheated greenhouse.

CHERRY AND SMALL FRUITED
Sweet Million F1

A cordon with many small red cherry fruits: a red-fruited alternative to orange Sungold.

NOVELTY
San Marzano

A plum tomato for sauces and cooking rather than fresh salads. Give it warm, protected conditions.

BUSH
Red Alert

An early bush cherry tomato for greenhouse beds or pots. Leave the side shoots to grow.

text:
Tomato, Greenhouse.
DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Greenhouse tomatoes offer flavours rarely found in shops. Cordons grow tall: train one main stem up a cane or string, removing side shoots. Bush types branch naturally; normally leave their side shoots and growing tips intact. Both need bright light, steady moisture and good ventilation. Pots and growbags dry out quickly.

Quick facts
Harvest

Jul – Oct

Germination

8–11 days

Yield per plant

8 lb

Plant under glass

Apr–May once warm.

Ready in

About 16 weeks from sowing

Sow indoors

Late Feb–Mar. Late Jan only with a heated greenhouse and bright light.

Containers

One per 12–18 in. pot, two per standard growbag.

18–24 in., wider for vigorous cordons.

Recommended varieties
CHERRY AND SMALL FRUITED
Sungold F1

A vigorous cordon tomato with very sweet orange cherry fruits. A strong first choice for greenhouse snacking and salads.

ORDINARY
Alicante

A traditional red salad tomato grown as a cordon. Retain as an accessible, general-purpose greenhouse variety.

F1 HYBRID
Shirley

An early cordon tomato producing medium red fruits under glass. A familiar, practical choice for an unheated greenhouse.

CHERRY AND SMALL FRUITED
Sweet Million F1

A cordon with many small red cherry fruits: a red-fruited alternative to orange Sungold.

NOVELTY
San Marzano

A plum tomato for sauces and cooking rather than fresh salads. Give it warm, protected conditions.

BUSH
Red Alert

An early bush cherry tomato for greenhouse beds or pots. Leave the side shoots to grow.

Key risks
Blight

Tomato blight causes brown lesions on leaves and stems, followed by fruit decay and plant collapse in favourable damp conditions.

Greenhouse whitefly

Whitefly adults and immature stages suck sap; sticky honeydew can support black sooty mould.

Blossom end rot

A dark, leathery patch at the flower end of the fruit results from insufficient calcium reaching developing tissue, often because root moisture fluctuates.

Split fruit

Irregular watering, particularly soaking after severe drying, can split ripe fruit.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
92
FRUITING CROPS

Water steadily and ventilate.

Even root moisture and moving air help fruit develop without splits or mould.

Train to the variety’s habit.

Remove side shoots from cordons; leave bush side shoots to grow.

Sowing & planting
Grow on in a pot
Plant and support
Sow indoors 

Sow thinly in trays or small pots of seed compost at about 64°F. Keep moist and give emerging seedlings plenty of light.

Prick out and pot on 

Move tray seedlings into pots at their first pair of true leaves. Support the roots and hold a leaf. Pot on as the roots fill the pot.

Plant in the greenhouse 

Wait until nights stay around 50°F or warmer. Water well-rooted plants and set them slightly deeper in pots, growbags or an enriched bed. Stand cordon pots 24 in. apart centre to centre. Support plants with canes or string.

Soil & preparation
Use fertile, well-drained border soil with added compost, or suitable pots/growbags of fresh peat-free compost.
Avoid waterlogging and stale, humid air. Containers need closer watering and feeding than a well-prepared border.
Looking after the crop
Tie cordons loosely; remove young side shoots. Take yellow lower leaves sparingly. Stop two leaves above the last useful truss, often in August under unheated cover. For semi-determinate varieties, follow the seed packet.
Water evenly and feed organically at the product rate as fruit develops. Ventilate in heat and gently tap flowering trusses. Reduce water as autumn growth slows.
Harvesting & storage
Pick fully coloured fruit gently; use promptly. Before cold ends the crop, bring sound unripe fruit indoors. Ripen at room temperature, checking trays for decay; a nearby ripe apple or banana can help ripen the remaining tomatoes.
Pests & diseases
Problem · what to look for	What to do
Blight — Brown leaf lesions; fruit may rot.	Remove infected plants; keep leaves dry and ventilate.
Greenhouse whitefly — White flies, sticky leaves and sooty mould.	Identify early; use suitable biological control.
Blossom end rot — Dark leathery patch at fruit base.	Keep roots evenly moist, especially as fruit swells.
Split fruit — Skins crack after uneven watering.	Keep moisture steady; avoid drying then flooding.
Tomato leaf mould — Yellow patches above; brown mould below.	Remove infected leaves; ventilate; keep foliage dry.
Aphids — Colonies on young growth.	Squash damaging colonies and encourage predators.
Grey mould (Botrytis) — Grey fuzz on damaged fruit or stems.	Remove infected tissue and dead material; ventilate.
Blossom drop — Flowers wither and fall without setting.	Water steadily; ventilate in heat; gently tap trusses.
Virus — Mottled, distorted leaves. Stunted plants.	Remove affected plants; clean hands/tools; monitor aphids.
Final tips

Remove lower leaves as the plants grow tall: this aids ventilation and the extra light will help the lower fruit to ripen.

Mulch soil beds and growbags with compost or well-rotted manure as the plants grow; tomatoes are heavy feeders.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
See also: Vegetable Troubles 139–143 · Growing Techniques 149–150 · 167 · 169–171
93
FRUITING CROPS

amendments.sourceNote: Book-only revision. Expand the introduction to explain cordons and bushes, using canonical greenhouse and outdoor tomato descriptions of their growth habits. Replace vague reminder and care qualifications with actionable copy. Keep January pale: the canonical late-January heated-greenhouse exception is corroborated by Garden Organic; specify the heated greenhouse and bright light in Quick facts. Late February–March remains the normal sowing period, supported by RHS. Retain all five varieties and add the canonical bush variety Red Alert, with greenhouse suitability corroborated by RHS and Thompson & Morgan. Shorten the two neighbouring lower-row descriptions to preserve meaning at three-column width. Apply John’s soil and ripening wording. John explicitly requests the two replacement Final tips and icons in the core JSON. Apply his wording verbatim in the working spread; the guarded save receipt binds the core care and Final tips changes. Other earlier book changes remain book-only. John’s latest book correction removes the healthy-leaves feeding/shading clause from the care paragraph to avoid conflict with Final tips. This is a working-page deletion; the previous guarded core-data save remains unchanged.
